summary: Mu'adh ibn Jabal (RA) was one of the most learned companions of the Prophet ﷺ, described by the Prophet himself as the most knowledgeable of the ummah in what is permissible and forbidden (halal and haram). He accepted Islam as a young man in Madinah, participated in all the major battles, and was sent by the Prophet ﷺ as a teacher and judge to Yemen. He was among the four companions designated as primary Quranic authorities, and he died in the plague of Amwas during the caliphate of Umar (RA) at approximately 33-38 years of age.
biography:
Mu'adh ibn Jabal ibn Amr ibn Aws al-Khazraji al-Ansari was born in Madinah around 603 CE, from the Banu Salama sub-clan of the Khazraj tribe. He accepted Islam as a teenager, still in his youth, at the hands of Mus'ab ibn Umayr (RA) before the Prophet's Hijrah to Madinah — making him among the earliest of the Ansar to embrace Islam, at approximately 18 years of age. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Vol. 1) that Mu'adh was exceptionally handsome in appearance, of fair complexion, and distinguished by an extraordinary brightness in his face — which the early scholars associated with the light of knowledge and worship.

Mu'adh participated in the Pledge of Aqabah through which the Ansar formally committed to the Prophet ﷺ, and he fought at the Battle of Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq, and all the subsequent major campaigns of the prophetic period. Despite this active military record, he became renowned above all for his scholarship. The Prophet ﷺ made a series of statements about him that are among the most direct prophetic attestations of a companion's scholarly standing. The most famous of these, narrated in al-Tirmidhi's Sunan (Kitab al-Manaqib — graded sahih by al-Albani): 'The most knowledgeable of my ummah in what is permissible and what is forbidden is Mu'adh ibn Jabal.' He also designated Mu'adh as one of the four primary authorities on the Quran: 'Take the Quran from four persons: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Quran).

The most consequential episode in Mu'adh's career was his appointment as the Prophet's ﷺ emissary to Yemen. In approximately 9-10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ dispatched Mu'adh to Yemen as a teacher, judge (qadi), and leader of the Muslim community there. Before his departure, the Prophet ﷺ gave him famous instructions that became a foundational text in Islamic legal methodology (usul al-fiqh). The Prophet asked him: 'How will you judge when a matter is brought before you?' Mu'adh replied: 'I will judge by Allah's Book.' The Prophet asked: 'And if you do not find it there?' He said: 'Then by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah.' The Prophet asked: 'And if you do not find it there?' Mu'adh replied: 'I will engage my own reasoning (ijtihad) and not fall short.' The Prophet ﷺ struck his chest and said: 'Praise be to Allah who has guided the emissary of the Messenger of Allah to what pleases the Messenger of Allah.' (Sunan Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Aqdiyyah; graded hasan by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in Fath al-Bari). This exchange established the three-tier hierarchy of Islamic legal sources — Quran, Sunnah, then ijtihad — and Mu'adh's name is permanently attached to this crucial methodological precedent.

In Yemen, Mu'adh served with distinction. He taught the Yemeni converts the Quran, the pillars of Islam, and the rulings of fiqh. He collected zakat and sent it to Madinah. He adjudicated disputes. The period he spent in Yemen cemented his reputation as the model for what a Muslim scholar-teacher-judge should be — learned in the primary sources, capable of independent reasoning, and dedicated to the welfare of the community he served.

Mu'adh returned from Yemen after the death of the Prophet ﷺ in 11 AH and subsequently participated in the Islamic expansion into Syria (al-Sham) during the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar (RA). He was appointed by Umar as a teacher and religious authority in Syria. It was during his time in Syria that the catastrophic plague of Amwas (Plague of Emmaus) struck in 18 AH (639 CE), killing tens of thousands including many senior companions. Mu'adh ibn Jabal died in this plague at approximately 33 to 38 years of age — a relatively young death that deprived the ummah of one of its greatest scholars. His death is recorded as a profound loss in the narrations of the companions and their successors. Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) reportedly wept and said upon hearing of the deaths in the plague: 'Would that Abu Ubayda were alive among us,' and the same grief extended to Mu'adh.

Al-Dhahabi devotes substantial space to Mu'adh in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Vol. 1), describing him as 'the Imam of the scholars' of his generation, noting that despite dying young he left a permanent impact through his students and through his legal methodology. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat (Vol. 3) records his biography with extensive detail. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in al-Isabah praises him as one of the most learned of the companions in jurisprudence. His approximately 157 narrations in the hadith collections span fiqh, Quranic interpretation, and the Prophet's personal character.
